architect.rationale: Two independent reasons, either one sufficient. (1) FILE OVERLAP, independent of isolation: four of the five work items must edit graph_agents/CURRENT-STATE.md (changelog / gap #1 correction / gap #7 closure / decisions row) and two must edit graph_agents/GRAPH.md (S3 state contract, S2 stop-rule note on degraded mode). Per architect.md:18-24 and GRAPH.md:84, slices that touch the same files are not a diamond, they are a sequence. I cannot name 3 disjoint file sets here, so it is not a diamond. (2) NO ISOLATION, NO ROLLBACK: scout facts 3+4 confirm neither repos/ nor graph_agents/ is a git repo, so feature-graph/SKILL.md:63 isolation worktree is unexecutable and architect.md:28 (one slice = one builder = one branch) is unsatisfiable for this target. Even after s1 creates a repo, this run would be the first-ever execution of builder/reviewer/integrator (CURRENT-STATE gap #2) AND a self-modification of the agent definitions the orchestrator spawns from. Proving worktrees, proving three untested nodes, and rewriting the spawn definitions in one run is stacking three unvalidated things on each other. Single-loop, sequential, one commit per slice.

isolation_decision.b_git_init: git init INSIDE graph_agents/ only. Doctrinally permitted, NOT a reversal of a logged decision. The logged decision (CURRENT-STATE.md:114) is 'Holding company, not monorepo - each app its own git repo', and CLAUDE.md:3-4 says repos/ is deliberately not a repo. The stated reason is that a root repo would swallow all five apps into a monorepo. graph_agents/ is itself a node in the portfolio graph (CLAUDE.md:41-43, GRAPH.md:18-20) and contains zero app code, so giving it its own repo is the SAME rule every other node already follows, not an exception to it. repos/ stays un-repo'd and s1 asserts that as a done_when check.
isolation_decision.d_docs: Fix feature-graph/SKILL.md and architect.md to describe degraded mode honestly instead of promising isolation they cannot deliver.
isolation_decision.c_snapshot_copy_rejected: A copy-the-directory substitute reintroduces every problem git worktrees solve (merge, conflict detection, diff) with none of the tooling, and it is a second mechanism to maintain forever. Once s1 lands, real worktrees are available for FUTURE fleet runs; this run does not need them because it is single-loop.
isolation_decision.a_force_single_loop_partially_adopted: Adopted as a standing rule for any run whose target is .claude/agents/** or .claude/skills/** - not because of git (s1 fixes that) but because of self-modification. Written into feature-graph/SKILL.md by s5.
isolation_decision.what_happens_when_a_builder_corrupts_an_: Before s1: nothing. The file is gone and must be retyped from memory. That is exactly why s1 runs first and alone, before any agent file is touched. After s1: `git -C graph_agents checkout -- .claude/agents/<file>.md` restores one file and `git -C graph_agents reset --hard HEAD` restores the whole fleet. The builder commits after each slice, so the blast radius of any single bad edit is one slice.

self_modification_protocol.rule: The plan is correct under BOTH answers because no slice's correctness depends on an edited definition taking effect during this run. s2 rewrites architect.md/reviewer.md/ops.md and s5 touches feature-graph/SKILL.md; no later slice in this run spawns an architect, an ops node, or re-enters the skill. The only agent spawned after s2 is the reviewer for the whole loop, and it reviews a DIFF - it reads the new reviewer.md as data either way, and its verdict does not change depending on which copy of its own definition was loaded at session start. Concretely: builder.md is edited by exactly one slice (s3) and only additively (record a branch field), so the question 'does a later builder see the new builder.md' never becomes load-bearing.
self_modification_protocol.handoff: s5 must write into CURRENT-STATE.md an explicit rule: after any run that edits .claude/agents/** or .claude/skills/**, START A FRESH SESSION before running the fleet again, because registration happens at session start (CURRENT-STATE.md:70-72). Do not assume this session is running the definitions now on disk.

plan.intent: Close gap #7 with machinery instead of more prose. Write graph_agents/.graph/verify-state.py: it takes a run-id (or a path to a state.json) plus one or more required node key names, and exits 0 only if every named key exists AND is non-empty - where a dict whose values are all empty strings or empty lists counts as NOT written, which is exactly the current shape of the untouched integrator key. Then wire it into feature-graph/SKILL.md at steps 2, 3, 5 and 6: after each node returns, the orchestrator runs it and does not advance until it exits 0. This does not stop the orchestrator hand-writing state (CURRENT-STATE.md:86-87); it makes silent non-writing detectable, which is the actual gap.

architect.edges: STRICTLY SEQUENTIAL s1 -> s2 -> s3 -> s4 -> s5. One builder, one context, one commit per slice. s1 -> everything: the real artifact is the git repo plus the initial commit, which is the ONLY rollback path for every later edit; nothing may edit a fleet file before it exists. s2 and s3 -> s5: the real artifact is the changed agent and schema files that the CURRENT-STATE.md changelog and gap list must describe - writing the snapshot before the changes exist would make it fiction. s4 -> s5: the real artifact is verify-state.py, which must exist on disk before GRAPH.md section 3 and gap #7 can point at it. Honest note on fake edges: s2, s3 and s4 have nearly disjoint file sets and would be parallel if isolation existed. They are ordered here because there is one builder and no isolation, so ordering costs nothing and removes the last collision surface. s1 and s5 are real edges; the s2/s3/s4 ordering is a degraded-mode concession and is labelled as such rather than dressed up as a dependency.
not_doing: NOT enforcing the umbrella invariant (gap #5). A cross-app-import linter is real engineering with its own design questions - which languages, what counts as an import, where it runs with no CI - and it is about APPS, not about the agent graph. It deserves its own run. Explicitly out of scope.

NOT running a diamond to prove diamonds work. Gaps #2 and #3 stay open on purpose. Proving fan-out belongs on a real app with a real git repo and a real test suite - huntstack - not on the fleet own definitions.

NOT touching the staleness hook or flag-stale-state.py. CURRENT-STATE.md:119 records a user-confirmed decision that it flags and never auto-stamps. Not revisiting it, not extending it, not making it block.
NOT adding, removing, renaming or re-tiering any node. Six nodes stay six nodes, scout stays haiku, nothing is downgraded, and no new critic or planner node is invented.

NOT rewriting architect.md wholesale. Judged honestly: its shape logic (lines 11-24), its delete-fake-edges rule and its Return block are sound and were load-bearing in this very run. Its real defects are exactly three - no state contract, a false claim about branches, and a done_when rule with no answer for Markdown - and s2 fixes those three. A rewrite would churn a file that mostly works.
NOT changing human gate placement or adding new gates.
NOT creating a git remote, pushing, or making repos/ a git repository. s1 explicitly asserts repos/ is still not a repo.
NOT touching anything outside graph_agents/. None of the five app repos are read or modified by any slice.
NOT building a snapshot-copy isolation mechanism (option c). Rejected with reasons recorded in isolation_decision.

NOT resolving whether Claude Code reloads agent definitions mid-session (scout risk 6). The plan is designed to be correct under either answer instead of depending on the answer. Resolving it is a separate experiment run.
NOT auto-updating CURRENT-STATE.md Last verified without a real re-check.
NOT touching portfolio/registry.json or the new-app skill.

If you read that prohibition as covering the whole tree, say so and I will replan around options (a) plus (d) only - but then the fleet permanently has no rollback and every future fleet-targeted run is single-loop by necessity, not by choice. s4.notes: WOULD IT HAVE CAUGHT ANYTHING IN THIS RUN? NO -- honest answer, unchanged. Every node in 2026-08-25-fleet-hardening (scout, architect, three builders, three reviewers) did write its own key, so no real failure in this run would have been caught. Its value is prospective: it turns the orchestrator's manual after-every-node read (done by hand five times this run, CURRENT-STATE.md:86-87) into one command, and after the attempt-2 fix it is RED on a freshly opened run instead of green. WHICH KEYS FAIL TODAY, PRECISELY -- s5 should copy this rather than summarise it: on this run, `integrator` fails as empty and `ops` fails as an untouched placeholder; on the parked run 2026-08-25-refuge-freshness, `builders.s1` and `reviews.s1` are absent while `ops` and `approved_by_human` are untouched placeholders. CORRECTION TO ATTEMPT 1: that note wrongly implied the script flags un-run nodes generally. It did not flag `ops` at all until the placeholder check existed, because {gated: true} is a non-empty boolean. WHAT IT STILL DOES NOT CHECK, so s5 does not oversell it: (1) CONTENT CORRECTNESS -- a key holding {"status":"done"} and nothing else passes; (2) KEY SHAPE -- it consults _schema.json for placeholder IDENTITY only, never for structure, so a missing `branch`, a missing `verdict` or an invented field all pass; (3) WHO wrote the key -- state.json records no authorship, so the never-rewrite-another-node's-key contract it is named after is invisible to it, and the orchestrator hand-writing every key still passes; (4) STALENESS -- no timestamps, so a key left over from a previous attempt passes; (5) numbers and booleans are non-empty BY DESIGN (a real parallel_safe:false must not look unwritten), so a hand-written {"gated": false} that differs from the template passes; (6) PARTIAL placeholders -- identity is compared on the WHOLE value, so a builders.<slice> where `status` was filled in but `branch` is still the template's description passes; (7) it is ADVISORY, not enforcing -- nothing invokes it automatically, no hook fires it, and it lives in a SKILL.md step the orchestrator has to choose to run. It is a check, not a gate. DESIGN NOTES: emptiness is recursive (a dict or list whose values are all empty is empty); the run path and the template path both resolve from the script's own location, so cwd does not matter, and a direct path to a state.json is accepted as the first argument. OUT OF SCOPE, NOT TOUCHED: (a) _schema.json stays as-is per the orchestrator's explicit instruction -- the self-documenting placeholders are s3's deliverable, and placeholder-identity detection survives template drift where blanking would not; (b) the .gitattributes / core.autocrlf noise flagged by s1, s1's reviewer and s3 is still unowned -- verify-state.py and this state.json are LF on disk and were rewritten preserving LF; (c) GRAPH.md and CURRENT-STATE.md are s5's and untouched -- s5 documents this script, I only built it; (d) builder.md:3's false 'in isolation / in parallel' frontmatter claim, raised by s3's reviewer, is still in no slice's file set; (e) step 5's verify-block placement -- the s4 reviewer ruled it is not a defect and restructuring step 5 belongs to s5.

PYTHON TRACEBACK on a state.json that is not valid UTF-8. open(path, encoding=utf-8) plus 'except json.JSONDecodeError' does not catch UnicodeDecodeError, which is raised inside json.load during fp.read(). Reproduced: a state.json encoded UTF-16LE-with-BOM prints a 12-line traceback ending 'UnicodeDecodeError: utf-8 codec cannot decode byte 0xff in position 0' instead of the documented one-line message. Not a contrived encoding: powershell.exe -NoProfile with output redirection on this machine emits ff fe 7b 00 ... (verified by od), and PowerShell is the primary shell in this environment. Any node or orchestrator that writes state.json with redirection or Out-File in Windows PowerShell produces a file that makes the verifier traceback. The exit code is still 1 so there is no false pass, but a traceback reads as 'the checker is broken' rather than 'the state file is corrupt'. FIX is one word: UnicodeDecodeError and json.JSONDecodeError are both ValueError subclasses (verified), so 'except ValueError as exc' at line 48 catches both; opening with encoding=utf-8-sig would additionally absorb the BOM case.
